clips.title: Vietnam made $99 a person in 1990. Now it's passed Indonesia #Shorts
clips.desc: In 1990 Indonesia was almost 6× richer per person. In 2025 Vietnam passed it (World Bank).

clips.hook: A third of the people, *more exports*
clips.title: Vietnam exports more than Indonesia with a third of the people #Shorts
clips.desc: Exports ≈ 98% of Vietnam's GDP vs 23% in Indonesia (World Bank, 2025).

clips.title: Indonesia now mines 2 of every 3 tons of nickel on Earth #Shorts
clips.desc: After banning raw ore exports in 2020 (USGS 2026).

clips.title: Why Vietnamese workers beat richer countries #Shorts
clips.desc: World Bank Human Capital Index: Vietnam 0.69, Indonesia 0.54.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.narration: In 1990, Vietnam was one of the poorest countries on Earth. {p} At market exchange rates, its economy produced less than a hundred dollars per person, for the whole year. Indonesia, its big neighbor to the south, produced almost six times as much. {p} Even adjusted for prices, Indonesia was two and a half times richer. {pp} In 2025, for the first time in the World Bank's records, Vietnam passed it. And even in plain dollars, it's now ahead, by about six dollars a person.

Vietnam had just come out of decades of war, and America kept a trade embargo on it until 1994. {p} In 1986, its Communist leaders had given up on central planning, with reforms they called Doi Moi, renovation. But in 1990, the results were still hard to see. {p} Indonesia has oil, gas, coal, nickel, and almost three times as many people. {p} On paper, this race wasn't close. {p} So how did the poorer country win? {pp} <soft>And is Indonesia really losing?</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $), 1990 = 1×
shots.narration: Start with the speed. {p} Since 1990, output per person in Vietnam has grown more than six times, after inflation. Indonesia's has about tripled. Thailand's and the Philippines', even less. {p} Among Asia's big economies, only China grew faster. {p} In 1990, the average Vietnamese produced about a fifth of the world average, adjusted for prices. Today, about seventy percent. Indonesia went from about half, to about the same seventy. {pp} Vietnam's economy has grown almost seven percent a year, on average, for thirty-five years. In 2025 alone, it grew eight percent.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP growth, Indonesia (annual %)
shots.narration: Indonesia's problem is the opposite. It's stuck. {p} In every normal year since 2014, its economy grew between four point nine and five point three percent. Like clockwork. {p} Even Vietnam's slowest normal year in that stretch, 2023, at just under five percent, only matched Indonesia's typical one. {p} Five percent sounds fine. But at five percent, an economy doubles in about fourteen years. At Vietnam's pace, in about eleven. {pp} Indonesia's president, Prabowo Subianto, has promised eight percent. It hasn't come close.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · exports of goods and services (% of GDP)
shots.narration: The difference is what each country sells. {p} In 1990, exports were worth more than a third of Vietnam's economy. By 2025, they were worth almost as much as its entire GDP. {p} Indonesia went the other way: from about two fifths of its economy in 2000 to less than a quarter. Thailand, the region's old factory, sits in between. {pp} Vietnam turned itself into a factory for the world. Indonesia's economy runs mostly on what Indonesians buy from each other.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · merchandise exports (current US$) and population, 2025
shots.title: Goods sold abroad, 2025
shots.narration: Since 2015, Vietnam has sold more goods abroad than Indonesia, with about a third of the people. {p} In 2025, about four hundred and seventy billion dollars' worth, against Indonesia's two hundred and eighty. {pp} Per person, that's almost five times as much.

stats.label: as much per person as Indonesia

shots.src: Samsung share: SEAsia (5 Jul 2026), est. 45–50% of global output · World Bank WDI · high-technology exports (% of manufactured exports, 2023) · FDI net inflows (% of GDP, 2025)
shots.title: Made in Vietnam
shots.narration: Much of that is electronics. {p} About half of all Samsung phones are made in Vietnam. {p} High-tech goods are more than forty percent of Vietnam's manufactured exports. In Indonesia, under ten. {p} And relative to the size of its economy, Vietnam attracts almost three times as much foreign investment. {p} It joined the World Trade Organization in 2007, then signed trade deals with Japan, Korea, Europe and the Pacific.
Quick favor: if you're enjoying this, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} Now, why didn't Indonesia do the same? {pp} Because it didn't have to.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita (current US$) · fuel, ores and metals (% of merchandise exports, 2023)
shots.narration: Indonesia sits on some of the world's biggest piles of coal, palm oil and minerals. It's the world's largest producer of palm oil, and one of the largest exporters of coal. {p} In 2023, almost a third of everything it exported was fuel, ores and metals. In Vietnam, about two percent. {p} Commodities pay well, until they don't. {pp} When commodity prices slid after 2012, Indonesia's income per person, in dollars, fell three years in a row.

shots.src: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 · nickel mine production 2025: Indonesia 2.6 Mt of 3.9 Mt world · Indonesia's raw nickel ore export ban (in force 1 Jan 2020)
shots.title: Indonesia's new bet: nickel
shots.narration: Now Indonesia is betting on a new rock: nickel, for electric car batteries. {p} In 2020, it banned exports of raw nickel ore, to force companies to process it at home. Later, it tried the same trick with bauxite. {p} It worked. In 2025, about two of every three tons of nickel mined on Earth came from Indonesia. {pp} But smelters are built with money, not with millions of workers.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · employment in agriculture (% of total employment, modeled ILO estimate)
shots.narration: There's one more ingredient, and it's people. {p} In 1995, seven in ten Vietnamese workers were farmers. Today, it's one in four, now fewer than in Indonesia. As late as 2010, almost half of Vietnam's workers were still on farms. {p} That's millions of people moving from rice paddies to assembly lines, where each worker produces far more. {pp} That shift, more than anything, is what growth looks like in a poor country.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · Human Capital Index 2020 (productivity of a child born today vs full education and health)
shots.title: Human Capital Index, 2020
shots.narration: And those workers arrive better prepared. {p} The World Bank's Human Capital Index estimates how productive a child born today will be, compared with one who gets a complete education and full health. It combines how long children stay in school, how much they actually learn, and how healthy they grow up. {p} A Vietnamese child: sixty-nine percent. {pp} An Indonesian child: fifty-four. {p} Vietnam even beats Malaysia and Thailand, which are far richer. In 2012, Vietnamese fifteen-year-olds outscored American and British students in math, on the OECD's PISA test.

But here's the twist: Indonesia isn't losing. {p} Its economy is still almost three times the size of Vietnam's, about one point four trillion dollars, by far the biggest in Southeast Asia. {p} And it has something Vietnam doesn't: a home market of almost three hundred million people. When foreign buyers stop ordering, Indonesians keep shopping. {pp} It has also quietly done something remarkable.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · poverty headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), Indonesia (% of population) · GDP growth
shots.narration: In 1990, almost eight in ten Indonesians lived on less than three dollars a day, adjusted for prices. {p} In 2025, fewer than four in a hundred. Inflation that year: under two percent. {p} And remember the Asian financial crisis? In 1998, Indonesia's economy shrank thirteen percent in a single year, and its currency lost more than two thirds of its value. {pp} It hasn't had a year anywhere near that bad since. Not even during the pandemic. {p} Vietnam's growth is faster. Indonesia's has been steadier.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · population aged 65+ (% of total) · fertility rate · GDP growth
shots.narration: So can Vietnam keep running? {p} Its biggest threat is time. Vietnamese women have about one point nine children on average, below the two point one needed to keep a population stable. Indonesia: about two point one. {p} People aged sixty-five and over are now almost a tenth of Vietnam's population. {p} That's about where Thailand was in 2013. {pp} Since then, Thailand's economy has grown only about two percent a year, and its population has started to shrink.

And Vietnam's model depends on customers abroad. Almost a third of what it sells goes to just one country: the United States. {p} One decision in Washington can change its whole year. {p} Indonesia's model is slower, but harder to break. {p} Vietnam is the sprinter. Indonesia is the marathon runner. {p} And both have picked the same finish line: 2045, a hundred years after each declared independence. Both say they want to be high-income countries by then. {pp} <soft>The next twenty years will show which one the world rewards.</soft> {p} Either way, a country that made under a hundred dollars a person in 1990 has already won something.
Want to see where falling birth rates lead? South Korea is already there. Watch this next. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Vietnam Overtook Indonesia. With a Third of the People.
yt.description:
In 1990 Vietnam produced less than $100 per person a year and Indonesia almost six times as much. In 2025, for the first time in the World Bank's records, Vietnam passed Indonesia in GDP per person adjusted for prices, and it's now ahead in plain dollars too. How the poorer country won (speed, exports, factories, people), why Indonesia didn't follow (coal, palm oil, nickel), and the twist: Indonesia's economy is still almost three times bigger, far more stable, and poverty there has nearly vanished.
